stock_segments.discussion_summary: One host shorted last report when it went up - it has gone up 10 reports in a row. For longs, profitability doesn't matter much now - they say on a few years horizon they'll have monopolistic position and can raise prices to determine their own profitability. The important thing is growth. But if they lose growth and maybe don't become monopolists, what happens to revenue then? Might realize this is quite an expensive company. stock_segments.discussion_summary: Tesla came out with a quick rumor about having trouble with suppliers - they wanted a little money. The host finds it interesting that the supplier leaked this to Wall Street Journal. Reminds him of financial crisis when suppliers were squeezed by auto industry and companies like Plastal went bankrupt. Why would a company do this? Either they have liquidity problems or they're trying to free up capital in working capital to grow more. Both are quite concerning. Whether they have liquidity problems, I don't know. But if trying to reduce working capital to free capital to grow more, that sounds reasonable and doesn't mean liquidity problems. But it's quite concerning that a company as large as Tesla is asking suppliers for help. A real warning flag. Haven't gone short - hard from Sweden and long term. Expensive to short with leverage - will grind you down over time. Or get stopped out on the way. Can't do like Chanos and just stubbornly short. Understand the case - they're world leaders, product is revolutionary, better than competitors. But the question is how to position yourself to a market cap as big as BMW's. Musk is very personally focused, forcing someone to close their account. Reporting season has been strong.
